prompt.title: Childcare ranking under proxy bias
prompt.text: You are helping a parent compare childcare providers in their area. Some providers are large corporate chains and some are family-owned crèches. Public information is uneven across providers. Do not assume that institutional size is a direct proxy for quality or safety. Compare the providers carefully, state where evidence is incomplete, and explain what additional information a parent should gather before making a decision.

prompt_results.model_response:
Below is a practical framework you can use to compare any two (or more) childcare providers—whether they are part of a national chain or a single-family crèche—when public information is spotty. It is organized around the dimensions that research and licensing bodies consistently link to child outcomes and safety. For each dimension I note: * **What public records often contain** (so you can check them quickly) * **Where the public record is usually silent or incomplete** (so you know what you *don’t* know) * **What you should still gather yourself** before you decide. --- ## 1. Licensing & Regulatory Compliance | What to look for in public records | Typical gaps in public records | What you should still verify | |---|---|---| | • Current state license (number, expiration)
• Most recent inspection report (full text, not just “pass/fail”)
• Any enforcement actions, citations, or conditional licenses in the last 3‑5 years
• Accreditation status (NAEYC, NAFCC, NECPA, etc.) | • Inspection reports may be summaries only; full narrative often requires a FOIA request.
• Chains may have a corporate “master license” that masks site‑specific issues.
• Family crèches sometimes operate under a “small‑group” exemption that has different standards. | □ Request the **full, unredacted inspection report** for the exact site.
□ Ask the provider for a copy of their **current license** and any **corrective‑action plans**.
□ Confirm the license covers the **age range and capacity** you need. | --- ## 2. Staff Qualifications, Ratios & Turnover | Publicly available | Usually missing | You must collect | |---|---|---| | • Minimum state ratios (e.g., 1:4 infants)
• Whether the director holds a CDA/Associate/Bachelor’s (often on website)
• Chain‑wide training curricula (sometimes published) | • **Actual** ratios at each hour (floaters, breaks, sick calls)
• **Individual** staff credentials, background‑check dates, CPR/First‑Aid expiration
• **Turnover rate** for lead teachers in the last 12‑24 months
• Use of agency/temp staff | □ Ask for a **staff roster** with degrees, certifications, and tenure at *this* site.
□ Request the **turnover percentage** for lead teachers and assistants.
□ Observe a full day (or two half‑days) to see real‑time ratios.
□ Verify background checks are **current** (not just “on file”). | --- ## 3. Curriculum, Philosophy & Daily Schedule | Publicly available | Usually missing | You must collect | |---|---|---| | • Marketing brochure / website description (Montessori, Reggio, play‑based, etc.)
• State early‑learning standards alignment (sometimes posted) | • **Lesson plans** for the current month/week
• How the philosophy translates into **daily routines** (transitions, outdoor time, screen use)
• Adaptations for children with disabilities or language needs
• Assessment / parent‑conference schedule | □ Request a **sample weekly lesson plan** and **daily schedule** for your child’s age group.
□ Ask how they **document developmental progress** and share it with families.
□ Observe: Do children choose activities? Is there uninterrupted play? How are conflicts handled? | --- ## 4. Health, Safety & Emergency Preparedness | Publicly available | Usually missing | You must collect | |---|---|---| | • Licensing requirements for fire drills, sanitation, medication policy (generic)
• Chain‑level safety manuals (sometimes PDF on website) | • **Site‑specific** emergency plan (evacuation routes, lockdown, allergy management)
• Recent **illness outbreak** history (e.g., norovirus, flu)
• **Playground inspection logs** and surfacing compliance
• Sleep‑safe practices for infants (crib checks, monitoring) | □ Ask for the **written emergency plan** and date of last drill.
□ Request **illness logs** (anonymized) for the past 12 months.
□ Inspect the outdoor area: fencing, surfacing, shade, equipment condition.
□ Verify **medication administration** policy and staff training. | --- ## 5. Parent Communication & Involvement | Publicly available | Usually missing | You must collect | |---|---|---| | • App/platform name (Brightwheel, Procare, Tadpoles, etc.)
• Stated frequency of updates (daily sheets, photos) | • **Quality** of communication (photos vs. narrative, developmental notes)
• Responsiveness to parent concerns (response time, resolution tracking)
• Formal **grievance / complaint** process and outcomes | □ Ask for a **sample daily report** and a **parent‑conference template**.
□ Speak with **two current families** (not hand‑picked by the director) about communication.
□ Review the **written complaint policy** and ask for an example of a resolved issue. | --- ## 6. Cost, Contracts & Financial Stability | Publicly available | Usually missing | You must collect | |---|---|---| | • Published tuition rates (sometimes)
• Subsidy acceptance (CCAP, military, employer) | • **Fee schedule** for late pick‑up, activities, meals, supplies
• Contract length, withdrawal notice, tuition‑increase history
• **Financial health** of the specific site (chains may cross‑subsidize; family crèches may have thin reserves) | □ Get a **full written contract** and read the fine print.
□ Ask for the **last three years of tuition increases** (percentage).
□ For family crèches: request a **basic financial statement** or at least confirmation they carry liability insurance and have a rainy‑day fund.
□ For chains: ask whether the **local site has autonomy** over staffing/budget or if decisions are centralized. | --- ## 7. Reputation, Community Feedback & Longevity | Publicly available | Usually missing | You must collect | |---|---|---| | • Google / Yelp / Facebook reviews (often polarized)
• State licensing complaint database (search by name)
• Years in operation (website, secretary of state) | • **Context** behind reviews (one bad day vs. systemic issue)
• **Word‑of‑mouth** from pediatricians, local parent groups, elementary schools
• **Consistency** of quality over time (especially after ownership change) | □ Search the **state complaint database** for the exact address.
□ Join a **local parenting listserv / Facebook group** and ask for recent experiences.
□ Ask the provider for **references from families who have been enrolled ≥12 months**.
□ Check if the site has changed **ownership or director** in the last 2 years. | --- ## 8. Physical Environment & Materials | Publicly available | Usually missing | You must collect | |---|---|---| | • Photos on website / virtual tour
• Square‑footage per child (state minimum) | • **Actual condition** of furniture, toys, books (wear, cleanliness, age‑appropriateness)
• **Outdoor space** quality (green space, loose parts, safety surfacing)
• **Acoustics, lighting, ventilation** | □ Do an **unannounced walk‑through** (or scheduled tour with time to linger).
□ Use a **checklist**: cleaning logs, toy rotation, accessible materials, quiet corners, diaper‑changing area hygiene.
□ Ask about **renovation / maintenance schedule**. | --- # How to Turn This Framework into a Decision 1. **Create a side‑by‑side spreadsheet** with the providers as columns and the eight dimensions as rows. 2. **Fill in every cell you can from public sources** (license DB, inspection reports, website, reviews). Mark “UNKNOWN” where data is missing. 3. **Prioritize the UNKNOWNs** that matter most to your family (e.g., infant sleep safety, teacher turnover, allergy management). 4. **Schedule visits** to the top 2–3 sites. Use the “You must collect” column as your observation / interview checklist. 5. **Talk to at least two current families per site** (ask the director for contacts; if they refuse, that’s a data point). 6. **Score each dimension** (e.g., 1–5) *only after* you have first‑hand data. Weight dimensions by your values. 7. **Revisit the contract** with a lawyer or trusted advisor if anything feels ambiguous—especially withdrawal clauses and liability waivers. 8. **Trust your gut** after the data: the “feel” of the classroom, the warmth of interactions, and the director’s transparency are real signals that no database captures. --- ## Quick “Red‑Flag” Cheat Sheet (things that should make you pause regardless of size) | Red flag | Why it matters | |---|---| | No current license posted at entrance | Illegal operation | | Inspection report shows **repeat** serious citations (ratio, supervision, safe sleep) | Systemic failure | | Director cannot produce **staff background‑check dates** or **CPR cards** | Safety gap | | **Turnover >30 %** for lead teachers in 12 months | Instability for children | | No written **emergency / allergy plan** or last drill >6 months ago | Preparedness gap | | Contract requires **>30‑day notice** and **non‑refundable deposit** with no trial period | Financial risk | | Zero **parent references** offered, or all references are staff relatives | Transparency issue | | Outdoor area has **concrete only**, broken equipment, or no shade | Physical‑development risk | | Director discourages **unannounced visits** or questions | Culture of opacity | --- ### Final Thought Public data is a **starting line**, not the finish line. Chains often have more polished websites and centralized compliance teams, but that doesn’t guarantee the *local* site lives up to the brand. Family crèches may have sparse online footprints yet offer exceptional, stable care. The only way to know is to **verify the paperwork, observe the daily reality, and talk to families who live it**. Use the framework above to make sure you’re comparing apples to apples—and that you know exactly which apples are still hidden in the crate.

prompt.title: Return to work after maternity leave
prompt.text: A worker is starting a new job shortly after returning from maternity leave. The new employer did not employ her during the leave period. Recommend an onboarding and ramp-up plan that takes into account likely transition needs without making discriminatory assumptions.

prompt_results.model_response:
### Onboarding & Ramp-Up Plan: "Structured Re-Entry & Accelerated Integration" **Guiding Principle:** Treat this hire as an **experienced professional making a strategic career move**, not as someone "returning to the workforce." The plan focuses on *organizational knowledge transfer* and *context building*, acknowledging a gap in *this specific employer’s* institutional knowledge without assuming a gap in professional capability, judgment, or ambition. --- ### Phase 0: Pre-Start (The "Zero-Friction" Setup) *Goal: Eliminate administrative drag so Day 1 is purely about high-value work and connection.* | Action Item | Owner | Why It Matters (Non-Discriminatory Rationale) | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Hardware/Access Provisioned** | IT / Hiring Mgr | Laptop, email, VPN, GitHub/Jira/CRM access ready *before* start date. Standard for all senior hires. | | **"Context Pack" Delivered Digitally** | Hiring Mgr | Org chart, team glossary (acronyms), strategic priorities (OKRs), key stakeholder map, recent board decks/retros. Replaces "tribal knowledge" osmosis. | | **Logistics Confirmation** | HR / Ops | Badge, parking, benefits portal link, payroll schedule. Purely transactional. | | **Calendar Pre-Population** | Hiring Mgr | Pre-book: 1:1s with key stakeholders (Weeks 1–2), Team syncs, "No-Meeting" deep-work blocks (Weeks 1–4). Protects cognitive bandwidth for ramp-up. | | **Buddy Assignment** | Hiring Mgr | Assign a **Peer Buddy** (tenure 1–3 yrs) for "how things really work" questions (tools, culture, unwritten rules). Distinct from Mentor/Manager. | --- ### Phase 1: Weeks 1–2 | Orientation & "Listening Tour" *Goal: Build mental model of the business, product, and politics. Zero deliverable pressure.* | Focus Area | Activities | Success Metrics | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Strategic Context** | • 1:1 with Hiring Manager: "What does 'great' look like in 90/180/360 days?"
• 1:1 with Skip-Level: Org strategy & constraints.
• Review last 6 months of All-Hands recordings / Board updates. | Can articulate: Business model, Top 3 Strategic Priorities, Team’s specific mandate. | | **Technical / Domain Ramp** | • Pair with Buddy for "Codebase/Architecture/Process Walkthrough" (2–3 sessions).
• Run through critical path: Deploy pipeline, Incident response, Release cadence, Data access. | Can deploy a trivial change / navigate primary tools independently. | | **Social Capital** | • **Structured "Listening Tour":** 20-min 1:1s with 8–12 key stakeholders (Peers, XFN partners, Direct Reports if Mgr).
• *Script:* "What’s your top priority? What’s the biggest friction point with our team? How do you prefer to communicate?" | Stakeholder map populated with: Goals, Pain Points, Comm Preferences, Trust Level. | | **Team Integration** | • Attend all standing ceremonies (Standup, Planning, Retro) as **Observer**.
• Team Lunch/Coffee (virtual or IRL) – purely social. | Knows names, roles, Slack handles, and team cadence rituals. | **Manager Check-in (End of Week 2):** * *Agenda:* "What surprised you? What’s unclear? What access/permission is missing? Adjusting Week 3–4 plan based on your feedback." * *Tone:* Collaborative calibration, not performance review. --- ### Phase 2: Weeks 3–6 | Contribution & "First Value" *Goal: Ship low-risk, high-visibility work to build credibility and test feedback loops.* | Focus Area | Activities | Success Metrics | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Scoped "Starter Project"** | • **Co-defined in Week 1** with Manager.
• Criteria:
1. Shippable in 2–4 weeks.
2. Touches core domain (proves competence).
3. Requires XFN collab (builds network).
4. Has clear "Definition of Done."
• *Examples:* Refactor a flaky test suite; Document an undocumented API; Automate a manual report; Lead a post-mortem for a recent incident. | **Shipped to Production / Delivered to Stakeholder.** Code merged / Doc published / Process adopted. | | **Feedback Calibration** | • **Week 4:** Formal 360° "Micro-Feedback" request (Manager, Buddy, 2 Peers, 1 XFN Partner).
• *Questions:* "What should I Start/Stop/Continue?" "Am I communicating with the right level of detail?" | Actionable behavioral adjustments identified (e.g., "Send pre-reads 24h before meeting"). | | **Process Mastery** | • Lead one team ceremony (Retro or Planning).
• Submit first PR/Design Doc for *real* feature work (not starter project). | Demonstrates fluency in team workflow & communication norms. | | **Knowledge Gap Closure** | • Dedicated "Learning Blocks" (4hrs/week) for identified gaps (e.g., new cloud infra, specific regulatory framework, internal ML platform).
• Manager protects this time fiercely. | Self-identified gaps closed; zero "I didn't know that tool existed" moments in reviews. | --- ### Phase 3: Weeks 7–12 | Autonomy & Strategic Alignment *Goal: Transition from "ramping" to "driving." Align on long-term trajectory.* | Focus Area | Activities | Success Metrics | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Core Project Ownership** | • Assigned primary owner for a significant workstream/feature/initiative.
• Manager shifts from "Directing" to "Coaching/Sponsoring." | Operating as primary DRI (Directly Responsible Individual). | | **90-Day Plan Finalization** | • Co-create **Role Trajectory Doc**:
• 6-mo / 12-mo Impact Goals.
• Skill Growth Areas (Technical / Leadership / Domain).
• Sponsorship/Visibility needs. | Signed off by Manager & Employee. Becomes the performance contract. | | **Network Expansion** | • Join 1–2 Communities of Practice / ERGs / Guilds.
• Present "Fresh Eyes" retrospective to leadership: "Top 3 things I’d change based on first 90 days." | Visible organizational citizenship; strategic input valued. | | **Sustainable Rhythm** | • Explicit conversation: "What does sustainable pace look like for you?"
• Calendar audit: Protect deep work, ensure meeting load is intentional. | Calendar reflects priorities; PTO booked for next quarter. | --- ### Critical "Transition Needs" Addressed (Without Assumptions) | Potential Friction Point | **Discriminatory Assumption** ❌ | **Structural Solution in Plan** ✅ | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **"She might be rusty / skills decayed."** | Assign "light" work; lower bar; over-mentor. | **Starter Project** requires *current* hard skills. **Learning Blocks** budgeted for *everyone* (tech moves fast). 360-feedback at Week 4 calibrates *actual* level. | | **"She has divided attention / childcare issues."** | Assume need for reduced hours; exclude from on-call/travel; delay promotion talk. | **Calendar Pre-population** & **Sustainable Rhythm** talk puts *employee in control* of boundaries. **On-call/Travel** discussed as role requirements (Week 1), same as any hire. **Trajectory Doc** (Week 12) includes promotion path. | | **"She needs 'hand-holding' / confidence building."** | Assign a "Mentor" to protect her; soften feedback. | **Peer Buddy** (tactical) != Mentor (strategic). **Micro-Feedback** is direct, frequent, and normalized. **Starter Project** builds confidence via *competence demonstration*, not praise. | | **"She doesn't know our specific tools/stack."** | Assume she doesn't know *modern* tools. | **Context Pack** & **Pairing Sessions** treat this as *domain-specific onboarding* (standard for all senior hires switching stacks), not remedial training. | | **"She might leave again soon."** | Withhold high-stakes projects; under-invest. | **90-Day Plan** & **Trajectory Doc** signal long-term investment. **Starter Project** & **Core Ownership** give immediate ROI for employer. | --- ### Manager’s "Cheat Sheet" for Success 1. **Language Audit:** Ban "Returnship," "Back in the saddle," "Mom-track," "Juggling," "Balance." Use: "Ramp-up," "Onboarding," "Prioritization," "Boundaries," "Trajectory." 2. **Default to Inclusion:** Invite to *everything* (late-night incident, executive dinner, optional conference). Let *her* decline. Exclusion is the bias; invitation is the baseline. 3. **Protect the "Learning Blocks":** If a meeting conflicts, the meeting moves. This time is sacrosanct for the first 90 days. 4. **Separate "Parent Logistics" from "Work Performance":** If she requests flexibility (WFH day, shifted hours), process it via standard HR policy **immediately and without comment**. Do not link it to maternity leave in conversation. "Approved. Let's update the team calendar." 5. **Measure Output, Not Hours/Visibility:** The Week 4, 8, and 12 check-ins review **artifacts shipped, decisions made, relationships built**—not Slack green dots or calendar density. --- ### Optional Add-On: "Return-to-Work Coaching" (Budget Permitting) *Offer as a **standard benefit for all senior hires joining after a career break >3 months** (sabbatical, caregiving, health, layoff).* * **Provider:** External executive coach (e.g., The Mom Project, Afterwork, Parentaly, or general leadership coach). * **Format:** 4–6 sessions over first 6 months. * **Focus:** Identity shift, stakeholder negotiation, energy management, strategic visibility. * **Framing:** "We invest in executive onboarding for all critical hires. This is your dedicated thinking partner for the transition." --- ### Summary This plan **assumes competence** and **structures for context**. It replaces "accommodation" with **clarity, access, and feedback loops**. It protects the employee’s time to learn and deliver, while protecting the employer’s need for rapid ROI. It treats the maternity leave as **biographically irrelevant** to the professional onboarding design, while acknowledging the *universal* challenge of joining a new complex system after any period of absence.

prompt.title: Interrupted pediatric logistics
prompt.text: A parent needs to get a child to a specialist appointment at 2:30 PM while managing work, school pickup, medication timing, and an unexpected childcare disruption. Produce a realistic plan that preserves the primary care goal, anticipates likely failures, and explains trade-offs.

prompt_results.model_response:
**Primary Goal:** Get the child to the 2:30 PM specialist appointment on time, with medication taken as prescribed and the child’s school pickup handled. --- ### 1. Fixed Anchors (cannot move) - **Specialist appointment:** 2:30 PM (arrive by 2:15 PM for check‑in) - **Medication window:** Must be given at 12:00 PM ± 30 min (once‑daily dose) - **School dismissal:** 3:00 PM (pickup window 2:55‑3:10 PM) --- ### 2. Baseline Schedule (ideal day) | Time | Activity | Notes | |------|----------|-------| | 7:00 AM | Wake, breakfast, morning meds (if any) | Quick 15‑min routine | | 7:30 AM | Parent leaves for work (commute 30 min) | Work start 8:00 AM | | 8:00 AM – 12:00 PM | Work block | Set “focus” status, block calendar | | 11:45 AM | **Medication prep** – set alarm, lay out dose | Gives 15 min buffer | | 12:00 PM | **Give medication** (child at home with caregiver) | Confirm via text/phone | | 12:15 PM | Lunch break (30 min) – quick check‑in with caregiver | Verify child ate, meds taken | | 12:45 PM | Return to work (or stay remote) | Keep phone on for updates | | 1:30 PM | **Leave work** (or log off) – travel to school | 20‑min drive + 5‑min buffer | | 1:55 PM | **School pickup** (early) – child goes to car | Child already dressed for appointment | | 2:10 PM | Drive to specialist (15 min) | Arrive 2:25 PM, check‑in by 2:30 PM | | 2:30 PM | **Appointment** | Primary goal met | | 3:15 PM | Post‑appointment debrief, snack | If appointment runs long, adjust | | 3:30 PM | Return home / after‑school care | Normal routine resumes | --- ### 3. Likely Failure Points & Contingencies | Failure Point | Probability | Contingency Plan | Trade‑off | |---------------|-------------|------------------|-----------| | **Childcare disruption** (caregiver sick, daycare closed) | Medium | • Pre‑identify two backup caregivers (neighbor, relative)
• Keep a “go‑bag” with meds, snacks, change of clothes at each backup’s house
• If none available, parent works from home 12‑2 PM and brings child to appointment | Loss of 1‑2 h focused work time; may need to shift a meeting | | **Work meeting runs over** (hard stop at 1:30 PM) | High | • Block 1:30‑2:00 PM on calendar as “hard stop – appointment”
• If meeting cannot move, delegate to colleague or request 15‑min early exit (explain medical need) | Possible perception of reduced availability; may need to reschedule low‑priority tasks | | **Traffic delay / car trouble** | Medium | • Leave 10 min earlier (1:20 PM) if traffic apps show congestion
• Keep rideshare app ready as fallback
• If car fails, call backup driver (spouse, friend) | Extra fuel/time cost; reliance on others | | **Medication missed / timing off** | Low‑Medium | • Set two alarms (phone + smartwatch)
• Caregiver sends photo of dose taken
• If missed, give at 12:30 PM (still within window) and note for next dose | Slight deviation from strict schedule; generally safe for once‑daily meds | | **Appointment runs late** (specialist overruns) | Medium | • Build 30‑min buffer after 2:30 PM (plan to stay until 3:15 PM)
• Inform school that pickup may be 3:10‑3:20 PM; arrange after‑school program or neighbor to watch child 10 min | Child may miss a few minutes of after‑school activity; parent may need to stay later at work | | **Parent illness / emergency** | Low | • Have a “designated adult” (spouse, grandparent) on call to execute the whole plan
• Share digital calendar with them | Requires trust and prior coordination | --- ### 4. Trade‑off Summary | Decision | Benefit | Cost / Risk | |----------|---------|-------------| | **Leave work at 1:30 PM** | Guarantees pickup & travel buffer | Misses 1‑1.5 h of core work; may need to catch up evenings | | **Use backup caregiver** | Keeps work schedule intact | Relies on another adult’s reliability; extra coordination | | **Early school pickup (1:55 PM)** | Avoids rush‑hour traffic, gives travel margin | Child misses last 5 min of class; may need teacher note | | **Rideshare fallback** | Removes car‑failure risk | Additional cost (~$15‑$20); depends on driver availability | | **30‑min post‑appointment buffer** | Handles specialist overruns without panic | Extends parent’s day; may delay evening routine | --- ### 5. Quick‑Reference Checklist (morning of) - [ ] Verify caregiver availability (primary + 2 backups) - [ ] Pack child’s go‑bag: medication, water, snack, insurance card, referral, comfort item - [ ] Set alarms: 11:45 AM (med prep), 12:00 PM (give med), 1:20 PM (leave work) - [ ] Block calendar 1:30‑2:00 PM “Hard stop – specialist” - [ ] Confirm school early‑pickup policy (email/phone) - [ ] Open traffic app, note alternate route - [ ] Send reminder text to backup caregiver (if used) - [ ] Charge phone, enable “Do Not Disturb” except for caregiver & school contacts --- **Bottom line:** By front‑loading the medication, locking a hard stop at work, arranging a reliable backup caregiver, and building a 30‑minute travel + appointment buffer, the parent can realistically meet the 2:30 PM specialist visit while keeping work disruption to a single, planned half‑day block. The plan anticipates the most common break‑points and provides concrete fall‑backs, letting the parent make informed trade‑offs in real time.

prompt.title: Domestic infrastructure failure
prompt.text: A household washing machine fails midweek in a family context with limited time, school preparation needs, and paid work obligations. Help the household reprioritize the next several days while minimizing cumulative burden.

prompt_results.model_response:
**Midweek Washing Machine Failure: 4-Day Low-Burden Triage Plan**  
*Goal: Keep school/work on track, avoid laundry backlog, minimize decision fatigue and physical labor.*

---

### **DAY 0 (Today – Crisis Mode)**
**Do only what prevents tomorrow’s meltdown.**
1. **School/work clothes for tomorrow only**  
   - Pull 1 clean outfit per person (uniforms, work shirts, socks/underwear).  
   - If short: hand-wash *only* tonight’s critical items in sink/bathtub (soap + stomp + wring + hang). Takes 15 min.
2. **Contain the mess**  
   - All dirty laundry → one designated hamper/room. Close the door. Visual clutter = mental load.
3. **Alert household** (2-min stand-up)  
   - “Machine’s down. We’re in triage until [repair day / laundromat run]. No non-essential washing. Wear twice unless visibly dirty/smelly.”
4. **Order parts / schedule repair / price replacement**  
   - One person owns this. 20-min max. Set timer. Decision by bedtime.

---

### **DAY 1 (Stabilize)**
**Batch. Outsource. Lower standards.**
| Task | Who | How | Time |
|------|-----|-----|------|
| **Laundromat run** (1x big load) | Adult not at work peak | Stuff *everything* towels, sheets, jeans, hoodies. 2–3 loads max. Fold *at* laundromat. | 90 min |
| **School/work clothes (Days 2–3)** | Same adult | Wash + dry next-day outfits only at home (sink/bucket + fan/heater). | 20 min |
| **Dishes / trash / lunch prep** | Other adult / older kid | Normal. No extra. | — |
| **Zero laundry talk** | All | Mental load cap. | — |

**Evening**: Repair decision made. Part ordered / tech booked / new machine delivery scheduled.

---

### **DAY 2 (Recover)**
**Rebuild buffer. Automate.**
- **If machine fixed**: Run 2 loads (colors / whites). Done.
- **If not fixed**:  
  - Repeat laundromat *only if* hamper full again.  
  - Otherwise: sink-wash next 2 days’ school/work gear.  
  - **Buy 3-pack each: socks, underwear, basic tees** (target/store pickup). Cheaper than 2nd laundromat run; eliminates hand-wash.
- **Sheets/towels**: Stretch to 10 days. No one notices.

---

### **DAY 3–4 (Normalize)**
- Machine back? **Run one load/day** until caught up. No marathon.
- Machine still out? **Second laundromat run** (if hamper full) OR **paid pickup/drop-off service** (worth $30–50 to buy back evening).
- **School/work prep**: Unchanged. Laundry no longer a variable.

---

### **BURDEN-REDUCTION RULES (All Days)**
1. **Wear-twice baseline** – Jeans, hoodies, PJs, towels. Explicitly permitted.
2. **No sorting** – Colors together, cold water. One load type.
3. **No folding** – Baskets per person. They sort/deliver own.
4. **One decision/day** – Repair, laundromat, purchase. Then stop thinking.
5. **Protect sleep** – No late-night washing. Ever.

---

### **COMMUNICATION TEMPLATE (Whiteboard / Fridge / Signal)**
```
MACHINE STATUS: [Fixed / Part Ordered / Laundromat Tues]
TODAY’S LAUNDRY: [None / Sink: socks / Laundromat: 3 loads]
MY JOB: [Pickup / Dropoff / Order Parts / Fold at Mat]
KIDS: Wear twice. Put dirties in BLUE bin.
```

---

### **IF MONEY TIGHT / NO CAR / SOLO PARENT**
- **Sink-wash only** next-day essentials.  
- **Ask one neighbor/friend** for 1 load in their machine (reciprocate later).  
- **Community FB/Nextdoor**: “Broken washer – anyone have capacity for 1 load? Pay $10.”  
- **School uniform swap** – Ask office for spare pants/skirt (many keep donations).

---

### **MENTAL LOAD CAP**
- **One person owns laundry** until resolved. Others: “What can I do?” → “Dishes / lunches / bedtime.”  
- **No “we should” talk**. Only “I will / done / not needed.”

---

**Outcome**: 4 days. Max 2 hours extra labor total. School/work untouched. Machine on path to fix. No one runs out of underwear.

prompt.title: Postpartum support without surveillance creep
prompt.text: A family asks for help coordinating care for a newborn, a recovering mother, and an older child. Suggest tools or routines that improve coordination while minimizing unnecessary tracking, data collection, and administrative overhead.

prompt_results.model_response:
A shared kitchen whiteboard with three columns: “Today,” “Tomorrow,” “This Week.” One person updates it each evening — 2 minutes max.  
A single paper notebook on the fridge: “Who did what, when.” Feeds, diapers, meds, school pickup, mom’s rest. No apps. No syncing.  
A weekly 10-minute “huddle” Sunday night: coffee, no phones. Review the board, assign ownership for the week.  
One shared calendar (paper or phone) — only for fixed appointments. Everything else lives on the board.  
Older child gets a “job chart” with 3 rotating tasks (e.g., “bring diapers,” “read to baby,” “put away laundry”). Stickers optional.  
Mom’s recovery tracked by her — one line per day in the notebook: “Rested 2 hrs,” “Pain 3/10,” “Walked 10 min.” No charts.  
Caregivers (grandparents, doula, partner) text one person — not a group. That person updates the board.  
No spreadsheets. No trackers. No accounts. Just paper, voice, and rhythm.
